name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

name: DeepLIFT
description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

name: Contextual Decomposition
description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

name: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
description: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) explains individual predictions by approximating the complex model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around a specific instance. It works by creating perturbed versions of the input (e.g., removing words from text, changing pixel values in images, or varying feature values), obtaining the model's predictions for these variations, and training a simple interpretable model (typically linear regression) weighted by proximity to the original instance. The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

name: Contrastive Explanation Method
description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

name: ANCHOR
description: ANCHOR explains one prediction of a black-box classifier with an if-then rule, called an anchor, such as 'age > 30 AND income < £50k'. An anchor names a small set of feature conditions under which the model keeps giving the same prediction, whatever the other features are. To find one, the method fixes the conditions, varies the other features by sampling, asks the model for a prediction each time, and searches for the broadest rule that holds in at least a chosen share of the samples, commonly 95%. Each anchor comes with its estimated precision and its coverage, the share of cases to which it applies. Both figures describe the model's behaviour on the sampled variations, not on real cases, and continuous features are first grouped into ranges.

name: RuleFit
description: RuleFit builds a predictive model that a person can read: a short list of if-then rules plus a few ordinary feature weights. It first trains an ensemble of decision trees (many small trees whose outputs are combined) and turns each branch into a candidate rule, such as 'IF age > 50 AND income < £30k'. It then fits a linear model over those rules and the original features using the lasso, a penalty that sets many weights to exactly zero, so only the most useful terms remain. The surviving rules and weights can be read directly, and each term has an importance score, overall and for single predictions. Fitted to real outcomes, the result can replace an opaque model; fitted to an opaque model's predictions, it is a surrogate that approximates that model, and its fit should then be checked.

name: Differential Privacy
description: Differential privacy puts a mathematical limit on what a published result reveals about any one person. The data holder adds random noise, drawn for example from a Laplace or Gaussian distribution, to each answer before release, such as a count, an average or a table of statistics, so the answer would look almost the same with or without any one person's data. The amount of noise depends on how much one person could change the answer (its sensitivity) and on a privacy budget called epsilon, which sets how far the two cases may differ (the Gaussian mechanism adds a second, small parameter, delta, for the chance of exceeding that limit). A smaller epsilon means more noise, a stronger guarantee and less accurate answers, and each release spends part of the budget. The guarantee covers whether a person's data took part, not conclusions about the wider population that the results legitimately show.

name: Conformal Prediction
description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

name: Platt Scaling
description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

name: Temperature Scaling
description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

name: Deep Ensembles
description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

name: Bootstrap Ensembles
description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

name: Jackknife Resampling
description: Jackknife resampling, also called leave-one-out resampling, shows how much a result computed from a dataset depends on any single record. The result can be a model's coefficients, its predictions or a performance score; it is recomputed n times on a dataset of n records, leaving out a different record each time and refitting the model where the result depends on one. The spread of the recomputed results, after a standard rescaling, estimates the bias and variance of the original result, meaning how far it would move with a slightly different sample. Records whose removal moves the result most are flagged as influential, and may be outliers or data errors worth checking. The method assumes the records are independent and that no single record changes the result abruptly.

name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board, also called an AI ethics board or AI review board, is a standing group from different disciplines that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects before they proceed. It differs from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because it also weighs harms to the people a system will affect and to society. Many boards first sort projects by risk, and for higher-risk work the project team submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, which members with technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds question and iterate on with the team. Where it has the power to decide, the board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects; where it only advises, it recommends one of these. It keeps a dated record of its decision, reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built, and some organisations share that record with an oversight body or publish it.

name: Red Teaming
description: Red teaming is a structured exercise in which a team deliberately tries to make an AI system fail, so that weaknesses are found before real users or attackers find them. The organisers set the scope and the harms of concern, recruit people with a mix of skills (for example security testers, domain specialists and members of affected groups), and give them a way to log each attempt and judge whether it worked. Participants try manipulative prompts, awkward edge cases and requests designed to draw out harmful, insecure or discriminatory responses, combining many approaches where a test for one known weakness, such as prompt injection, covers only one. The result is a record of the failures found and how easily each was provoked, which is not a pass or fail verdict. It feeds a risk register (the list of known risks and who owns them) and fixes, and the exercise is repeated when the system changes.

name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

name: Confidence Thresholding
description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

name: MLflow Experiment Tracking

name: Monotonicity Constraints
description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

name: Generalized Additive Models
description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

name: Concept Activation Vectors
description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

name: Knowledge Boundary Probing
description: Knowledge boundary probing maps what a language model can and cannot reliably answer. A probe set is built from questions across the topics the system will face, including some with known answers and some that cannot be answered. Each question is asked in several phrasings, because a model may answer one wording correctly and fail on another. Responses are scored for correctness, for whether the model signals doubt when it should, and for whether its stated or computed confidence tracks whether it is right. The result is a topic-by-topic map of what the model knows, knows only under some phrasings, and does not know, which informs where to deploy it, what to tell users about its limits, and where to add training data or human review.

name: Machine Unlearning
description: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training records from a trained model, so that the model behaves as if it had never seen them. It is used when someone withdraws consent or asks for deletion, for example under the right to erasure (the 'right to be forgotten') in data protection law, and retraining from scratch would be too slow or costly. Exact methods, such as sharded training, split the data into parts that each train their own sub-model, so a deletion means retraining only the sub-model that used those records, which gives a result statistically the same as retraining without them. Approximate methods instead edit the trained model directly to reduce the records' influence, which is faster but gives weaker assurance, and certified methods add a formal bound on how much influence can remain.

name: Out-of-Domain Detection
description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Scope is defined by examples, such as an assistant's supported intents (the actions it can recognise), and a detector then scores how closely each new query resembles them. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. A query judged out of scope can be declined, handed to a person or another service, or answered with a request to rephrase, instead of receiving an unreliable or invented answer. The detector tests resemblance to the defined scope, not what the system actually knows, so it needs evaluating on realistic out-of-scope queries.

name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

name: CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials
description: A CycloneDX ML-BOM (machine-learning bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of what a model is made of, written in the CycloneDX standard (ECMA-424) so that tools as well as people can check it. It applies the software bill of materials, a structured list of the components in a piece of software, to models: the model is declared as a component of type machine-learning-model with its identifiers, version, supplier, licence and file hashes, together with the base models it was derived from (its pedigree), the datasets used to train and evaluate it with their source, classification and owners, the libraries it depends on, and an optional structured model card giving its task, architecture, performance metrics, intended uses and known limitations. The BOM is written at release, by hand or with a generator that reads the model's repository and metadata, checked against the CycloneDX schema, and can be signed. Consumers then query it, for example to find every deployed model that uses a dataset or library found to be compromised, or to check a supplier's declared datasets and licences before purchase. Unlike a model card or datasheet, written for people to read, or an experiment log or data version history, which stay with the team that built the model, it is a parts list in a fixed schema that travels with the model and can be matched against vulnerability records and file hashes, but it records what its author declares and verifies none of it.

name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

name: Forward Simulation Test
description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

name: Actionable Recourse Audit
description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

name: AI FactSheets
description: AI FactSheets is a documentation practice in which the developer or supplier of an AI model or service answers a structured set of questions about it, modelled on the supplier's declarations of conformity that industries such as telecommunications and transport use to give written assurance, with evidence, that a product meets stated requirements. The questions cover the service's purpose and its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was trained and tested on, its test methods and results (reported for groups such as age bands or genders where relevant), checks for bias, explainability, behaviour on data unlike its training data and robustness to adversarial attack, how user data is secured, and its lineage, such as when and how its models were retrained; 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' are allowed answers. Facts are gathered from the people in each role across the lifecycle (business owner, data scientist, model validator and operations engineer), and any change to the service produces a new version of the FactSheet while earlier versions are kept. The originating group's seven-step method designs the template with its readers: interview the people who will read the facts and those who will produce them, draft and trial a template of questions, have the real producers complete it, evaluate the result with its readers for content and presentation, and build further templates for other audiences such as a review board or regulator. Unlike a model card, which reports one model's intended use and evaluation to the people choosing it, or a datasheet, which describes one dataset, a FactSheet may cover one model or a whole service built from several models and datasets (attaching their datasheets), gathers facts from each role in the lifecycle and has a different template for each audience; unlike a CycloneDX ML-BOM it is written for people to read rather than as a machine-readable parts list for software tools.

name: UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Record
description: An Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) record is a public account that a UK public sector organisation writes about one algorithmic tool it uses, on the UK government's standard template, and publishes in a central repository on GOV.UK. The template has two tiers: a short plain-language summary for the general public (what the tool is, why it is used and a contact), and eight further sheets for specialist readers such as journalists, researchers and civil society, covering who is accountable for the tool and which suppliers were involved, how it works and what it replaced, how its output feeds into decisions, when a person reviews that output, how members of the public can appeal, the system's and each model's inputs, outputs, architecture and performance (including any bias testing), the data used, and the impact assessments, risks and mitigations. Information that would be exempt under the Freedom of Information Act can be left out or summarised field by field, with the reason stated, and the record is cleared by the tool's team, its senior responsible owner (the role accountable for the tool) and the press office, checked for readability by the central ATRS team, and updated when the tool changes substantially or is retired. Publishing is mandatory for central government departments and for arm's-length bodies that deliver public or frontline services or deal directly with the public, for tools in beta, pilot or production that significantly influence decisions affecting the public or interact with it directly; other public bodies may publish voluntarily. Unlike a model card, written by a developer for people choosing a model, or a supplier's AI FactSheet for buyers, an ATRS record is written by the deploying public body for the public and describes the decision process, human review and appeal routes around the tool as well as the tool.

name: C2PA Content Credentials
description: C2PA Content Credentials attach a signed provenance record, called a manifest, to a media file, so that whoever receives the file can see who signed it and what the signer declares (which tool produced it, whether a generative AI model created or altered it and what edits followed), and can check that the record, and the parts of the file its hash covers, have not changed since signing. Under the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) technical specification, the tool that creates or edits the file writes statements called assertions, such as a 'created' action whose source type is trainedAlgorithmicMedia (the code for AI-generated content) and links to the earlier files it was made from, adds a cryptographic hash of the file's content, and signs the bundle with an X.509 certificate, the kind of credential used to secure websites. The manifest is usually embedded in the file, and each later edit in a supporting tool adds a new manifest that refers to the previous one, so the history travels with the file. A validator recomputes the hash and checks the signature, then reports the manifest as well-formed, valid or, if the signing certificate chains to a trust list such as the C2PA Trust List, trusted, and reports a failure when the file no longer matches its hash. If the manifest is removed, nothing in the file leads back to it unless a watermark or fingerprint (a 'soft binding') was also registered so that the manifest can be looked up in a repository, and a file without credentials says nothing about its origin; unlike trigger-set model watermarking or model signing, which mark or sign a model, it records the history of an individual output.

name: Zero-Knowledge Proof of Model Inference
description: A zero-knowledge proof of model inference lets the owner of a model show an outside party that one specific model, fixed in advance, turns a particular input into a particular output, without revealing the model's weights. The owner publishes a commitment to the weights, a short cryptographic fingerprint such as a hash that binds them without disclosing them, together with a verification key that fixes the model's architecture. The model's arithmetic is converted to whole numbers (quantised) and written as a system of equations called a circuit, and for each input a proving system produces a proof, of a few kilobytes to a few hundred kilobytes, that this circuit, run with weights matching the commitment, turns that input into that output; the input can be public or committed in the same way. Anyone holding the verification key can check the proof in milliseconds to seconds: it shows that the committed model gives that output for that input, while keeping the weights hidden, and says nothing about whether that model is accurate, fair or safe. Unlike homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on data it cannot read but gives the caller no evidence of which computation was run, and unlike model signing, which lets someone who holds a model's files check who released them, it lets someone who never sees the weights check individual outputs against them.
